title: Wild stock market swings: will I lose money, and is there anything I can do?
excerpt: Shares are volatile amid jitters over tech and AI – but think carefully before you decide to ditch investments too
content_html:
It has been a volatile time on global stock markets, with rapid rallies and punishing sell-offs. There have been signs in recent weeks that investors are getting cold feet over the outlook for AI companies and selling off technology stocks.

Last week, the AI company Anthropic launched on to the market and had a record-breaking first day, but on Friday stock markets around the world tumbled and the US Nasdaq closed 5% below its mark on 1 January.

On Monday, the dramatic return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia sent its shares soaring and contributed to a jump in US stock markets.
content_text: It has been a volatile time on global stock markets, with rapid rallies and punishing sell-offs. There have been signs in recent weeks that investors are getting cold feet over the outlook for AI companies and selling off technology stocks.Last week, the AI company Anthropic launched on to the market and had a record-breaking first day, but on Friday stock markets around the world tumbled and the US Nasdaq closed 5% below its mark on 1 January.On Monday, the dramatic return of Jensen Huang as chief executive of Nvidia sent its shares soaring and contributed to a jump in US stock markets.Why are the markets going down?Investors seem to be losing faith in AI – or rather in the valuations of companies that are involved in the industry. This month, several events have led to sell-offs – the surprise scale of the Democrats’ win in the US midterms was swiftly followed by Huang’s exit over an relationship with an alleged Chinese spy. The rapid offloading of tech stocks after these events suggests a jitteriness among investors.Will I lose money?Lots of people own shares that are falling in value, either through their pension or other type of investment account. Many of the shares that are experiencing the biggest falls are companies that have dominated indices and, as a result, the passive funds that track them.Dan Coatsworth, the head of markets at AJ Bell, says two of the most popular passive investments among investors are global equity funds and funds tracking the S&P 500 US stock market index. “Both have exposure to the giants of tech in a large way,” he says. And, as a result, both have fallen in recent days.Coatsworth says that, while 15 years ago US shares represented half of the MSCI World index – a benchmark for the global stock market – it is now 73%. Tech is the dominant sector and officially represents 30% of the index. However, Google’s parent Alphabet and Facebook’s owner Meta are classed as communication services stocks – adding them bumps up tech to about 35% of the index.Investors who think they have diversified by being in a global fund may be having a nasty surprise.Some tracker funds hold shares in tech companies such as Anthropic, which made its stock market debut last week. Photograph: Leonardo Muñoz/AFP/Getty ImagesThe investment platform interactive investor (ii) reports on the top holdings of its customers every quarter. Its most recent report shows global tracker funds are well-represented in their portfolios, as is Scottish Mortgage – an actively managed investment trust that holds shares in SpaceX, Nvidia and Anthropic, among others.However, an important thing to remember about falling share prices is that you do not lose money until you sell. Only at that point do you crystallise your loss.And you may not even have losses on paper, depending on when you invested. In recent years stock markets have been climbing. The FTSE 100 is still higher than it was last year. Scottish Mortgage has been falling since mid-October, but its shares are still well up on this time last year.What can I do?Resist panicking. Holly Mackay, the chief executive of the consumer website Boring Money, says: “Humans are programmed to fight or take flight when something goes wrong. However, this instinct to take action is often the worst response to falling markets when doing nothing is the most sensible response.”Coatsworth says recent sell-offs “may seem unpleasant, but it isn’t out of the ordinary. History shows that markets go through cycles and what’s unfolding in front of our eyes is par for the course.”He points out that markets bounce back, including after recent falls such as in April 2025 after Donald Trump’s tariffs announcement, and earlier drops fuelled by inflation and the Covid pandemic.Can I do anything?Camilla Esmund, the head of investor campaigns at ii, says this is a timely reminder to review your investment strategy and check the level of risk you are taking and whether you are sufficiently diversified.“It is wise to diversify your portfolio across sectors, regions, and asset classes, so no single shock derails your progress,” she says. “By doing this, you are spreading your risk and ensuring that you are not overexposed to one area of the market.”Coatsworth says if you are approaching retirement, “the key is to review your investments to make sure they are still aligned with how you plan to take an income from your pot.”How do I diversify to avoid further tech downturns?Coatsworth says there are a few paths to consider.“One way to dial down tech exposure is to switch into a global equity fund that excludes the US,” he says. “For example, iShares MSCI World ex-US ETF invests in a basket of companies from around the world excluding the US.”Tech stocks outside the US account for 10.9% of the portfolio, but the main holdings include banks, healthcare companies, oil producers and miners. “That would provide more sector balance and less dependence on tech, but it would mean some of the key names that have led the US market rally in recent years like Nvidia no longer being in the driving seat,” he says. However, if those stocks recover, you will be missing out on any potential gains.He says a possible “middle ground” is the Invesco MSCI World Equal Weight ETF. At the end of September, the US represented 40.6% of the investment – less than with a traditional global equity fund. “The investor still has their toe in the pond for US tech exposure, but they wouldn’t be up to their neck in the water,” he says.Should I buy the dip?Some people see falling prices as an opportunity. Earlier this month, the investment platform Hargreaves Lansdown reported that its clients had been buying overseas tech shares after the post-midterm falls.Mackay says there are many great tech companies which make a lot of money and have huge growth potential.“I expect some pain but I’m sitting tight and will actually look to buy into any quality companies which are unfairly punished as some rattled investors rush for any exit,” she says.
